                                       PROJECT NO. 58481

                                                  §
 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                                  §
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION
                                                  §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                                          OF TEXAS
                                                  §

              VISTRA CORPORATE SERVICES COMPANY’S COMMENTS

TO THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

        Vistra Corporate Services Company (Vistra) files these comments in response to the
Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC § 25.194 issued by the Public Utility Commission of
Texas (Commission) on March 12, 2026 (the PFP). The PFP set an April 17, 2026 deadline for
submittal of comments and thus, these comments are timely filed. An executive summary is
included in a separate attachment at the end of the comments.

                          I.      INTRODUCTION AND OVERVIEW

        Vistra reiterates and incorporates its prior comments in this rulemaking associated with
courtesy filings of Vistra’s Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 145 comments on March
20, 2026 and April 9, 2026. Whereas those prior comments specifically address concerns and offer
feedback for PGRR145 as a transitional process that includes some “cross-references” to
Project No. 58481, the specific comments in the following section are largely “post-transition” or
“steady state” in nature and are informed by, but not presumptive of, Batch Zero dynamics.
However, all three reflect a common theme: supporting co-location of generation and large loads,
particularly, net metering arrangements of new loads with existing generators subject to
PURA § 39.169 and the Commission’s new 16 TAC § 25.205 (“39.169 NMAs”). The
39.169 NMAs are a small subset of the large load interconnection queue, but have both
(1) specific statutory timing requirements and (2) unique flexibility, transparency, and cost-
effectiveness characteristics that warrant prioritization over the near-to-midterm planning
horizon. The Commission and ERCOT should prioritize and account for the unique
characteristics and procedural considerations of 39.169 NMAs in both Batch Zero
(PGRR145) and this rulemaking.

        Vistra’s prior comments on PGRR145 have highlighted concerns about the timing of
ERCOT’s proposed Batch interconnection study timeline, specifically as it relates to Batch Zero.


Vistra Comments || Project No. 58481                                                   Page 1 of 19
                                                                                                      1
 In summary, the plain language of PURA § 39.169(d) states that “[ERCOT] shall study the system
impacts of a proposed net metering arrangement and removal of generation for which the [ERCOT]
receives a notice under Subsection (a) after [ERCOT] receives all information regarding the
arrangement required by [ERCOT] to be submitted to [ERCOT]. [ERCOT] must complete the
study and submit the results to the commission with any associated recommendations not later
than the 120th day after [ERCOT] receives all required information regarding the arrangement.”
Importantly, note that the only reference to completion of a study in PURA § 39.169(d) is ERCOT’s
system impacts study – specifically, that it must be completed within 120 days of receiving the
necessary information to conduct the study.

        PURA § 39.169(d) could have said “ERCOT must study the system impacts after it has
studied the system impacts in a Batch study,” but it does not. Instead, the Legislature chose
language anchoring the 120-day clock for ERCOT to study system impacts, including transmission
security, which is a (if not the) core function of the Batch study “after [ERCOT] receives all
information regarding the arrangement required by [ERCOT] to be submitted to [ERCOT].”
Therefore, once ERCOT has all information about a 39.169 NMA necessary to evaluate it in a
Batch Study and conduct the required resource adequacy assessment, its statutory initiation
requirements are fulfilled, which triggers the 120-day statutory deadline.

        However, at the same time, the Commission’s recently-adopted Net Metering Arrangement
rule says in 16 TAC § 25.205 there are several provisions that would restrain a 39.169 NMA
proceeding from commencing until after the Large Load interconnection study is “completed.”
This creates a potential timing conflict with the ERCOT-conducted Batch study, unless the Batch
study can be completed within the 120-day window afforded in PURA § 39.169(d). As currently
drafted, however, PGRR145 in combination with 16 TAC § 25.205 could materially extend the
procedural timeline for 39.169 NMAs to receive approval to energize.

        Vistra has proposed reasonable mitigations for the timeline impact in its PGRR145
comments, namely:

    •   39.169 NMAs with an assigned Large Load Interconnection Number (LLI#) and initial
        energization date on or before December 31, 2027, as well as any 39.169 NMAs with
        applications approved or pending at the Commission, will be studied under the Legacy




Vistra Comments || Project No. 58481                                                  Page 2 of 19
                                                                                                     2
         Large Load Interconnection process retained in PGRR145’s Sections 9.9-9.10, and
        included in base load under PGRR145’s Section 9.2.1.1.

    •   39.169 NMAs with an assigned LLI# and initial energization date between January 1, 2028
        and December 31, 2028, and not already included in base load, will be included in Batch
        Zero as load to be studied and allocated in Batch Zero under PGRR145’s Section 9.2.1.2.

        The first bullet ensures that a 39.169 NMA with an initial energization date prior to Batch
Zero’s energization window starting in 2028, or that has a pending or recently-approved
39.169 NMA application before the Commission is not unnecessarily delayed in its energization.
This is pragmatic and respects both the statutory deadlines in PURA § 39.169 and the recently-
adopted rule requirements of the Commission’s 16 TAC § 25.205(d)(1)(B) because both the
interconnection study and the Commission’s NMA proceeding would need to be complete for such
projects prior to January 1, 2028 (when the first Batch Zero energization window opens). Vistra
appreciates the Commission’s recognition of the interplay between PGRR145, this rulemaking and
39.169 NMAs at the April 17, 2026 open meeting, and supports the approach suggested for
pending 39.169 NMAs in that discussion.

        The second bullet helps to minimize any delays to 39.169 NMAs with a 2028 initial
energization date by assessing those that are not already included in base load but have an assigned
LLI# in Batch Zero. This proposal is also pragmatic as it should broadly allow reconciliation of
ERCOT’s preference to have all incremental 2028+ energizations evaluated under the Batch
process with the PURA § 39.169(d) deadlines as implemented by 16 TAC § 25.205.

        Aside from statutory timing considerations, there are also strategic and reliability reasons
that the Commission and ERCOT should prioritize 39.169 NMAs in both the Batch Zero process
and in this rulemaking. First, as a threshold matter, the Batch process is going to determine which
large loads are able to energize in the near- and medium-term, and Texas is blessed to see
significant interest in investing in the state. Load flexibility over this transitional period is going
to be very important for managing the small number of hours when system conditions get truly
tight. 39.169 NMAs offer a unique blend of flexibility and transparency to system operators that
the PUCT and ERCOT should lean into.

        First, SB6 mandates 39.169 NMAs to provide load flexibility. While other large loads may
provide    flexibility   (e.g.,   through   the   voluntary   program     being    developed    under


Vistra Comments || Project No. 58481                                                       Page 3 of 19
                                                                                                          3
 PURA § 39.170(b)/Project No. 58482 – which could also include 39.169 NMAs), 39.169 NMAs
specifically can be required to provide flexibility in a manner approved by the Commission.
ERCOT views this flexibility as a very important tool in managing tight grid conditions and has
recommended that flexibility as a mandatory condition in each of its completed studies under
PURA § 39.169. 1 Vistra recognizes the importance of this flexibility, and has made a commitment
in the 39.169 NMA application for Comanche Peak Power Company LLC that the full capacity of
the Comanche Peak nuclear power plant will remain available to the ERCOT grid during
emergency conditions, supported by customer-owned backup generation facilities. 2 If forced to
prioritize among large load interconnections, this operational benefit to ERCOT will help to
enhance reliability while other large loads and associated infrastructure are developed to support
them.

        Second, 39.169 NMAs are among the most transparent large loads to system operators
since ERCOT can require real-time telemetry of both the load and the generator output, as well as
the net generator output through the generator’s Qualified Scheduling Entity (QSE). Broadly
speaking, ERCOT only has direct visibility into large loads that (1) register and operate as a Load
Resource (e.g., a Controllable Load Resource (CLR)); or (2) are netted with a generation resource
behind a common point of interconnection. Registering and operating as a Load Resource is
voluntary, and not every large load will choose to do so. However, Vistra expects that every large
load that is part of a 39.169 NMA will have real-time telemetry to ERCOT through the generator’s
QSE. This additional guarantee of reliability-enhancing operational visibility is another reason that
39.169 NMAs should be prioritized, all else equal.

        Third, 39.169 NMAs are likely to be more transmission-efficient than other large loads that
interconnect directly to the transmission system. Because existing generators already have
interconnecting transmission facilities, most 39.169 NMAs should not require new transmission
facilities to deliver power to the co-located large load, because the large load customer can build

Study Results and Recommendations, Application of Freestone Power Generation, LLC and C1 Freestone 1 LLC for
Approval of a Net Metering Arrangement, Docket No. 58872 (March 18, 2026).

Implementation, Docket No. 59399 (Feb. 19, 2026).


Vistra Comments || Project No. 58481                                                                   Page 4 of 19

 and operate its own self-use transmission facilities to deliver power from behind the generator’s
point of interconnection to the ERCOT transmission system. These privately-funded transmission
facilities are not included in rate base and are not at risk of having those costs allocated to other
customers.

        For all these reasons (statutory, operational flexibility and transparency, and cost-
efficiency), the Commission and ERCOT should prioritize 39.169 NMAs in Batch Zero, as
recommended in Vistra’s April 9, 2026 PGRR145 comments. Furthermore, the Commission
should similarly accommodate the unique characteristics and procedural considerations of
39.169 NMAs in this rulemaking. Vistra has proposed in the section below a few specific
recommendations to maintain the 120-day statutory study timeline, allow exclusivity agreements
to count for site control at Intermediate Agreement stage, and delay the requirement for the non-
refundable interconnection study fee for 39.169 NMAs from the Interconnection Agreement until
after the Commission decision in the 39.169 NMA application proceeding.

        Vistra’s specific comments on a selection of provisions in the proposed rule follow below.
Please note that the specific rule provision comments are grouped conceptually for brevity and
flow; a full redline is also provided as Attachment A, which also includes a few minor and likely
self-explanatory edits that are not addressed in these narrative comments for brevity.


                  II.      COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC RULE PROVISIONS

A. The rule should account for unique procedural considerations of 39.169 NMAs.

        1. Ensure interconnection studies for 39.169 NMAs comply with deadlines in
             PURA § 39.169(d).

        As discussed in Vistra’s prior filings in this rulemaking and briefly recounted in Section I
above, PURA § 39.169(d) establishes a 120-day window for ERCOT to complete its studies of
system impacts of 39.169 NMAs, including transmission security, after receiving all necessary
information    regarding     the   arrangement.   While    the   Commission’s      recently-adopted
16 TAC § 25.205 also applies a 120-day window to ERCOT’s completion of studies subsequent
to receipt of a 39.169 NMA notice and all information ERCOT requires about the 39.169 NMA,
the plain language of PURA § 39.169(d) still applies to ERCOT-conducted studies. Considering
that the timeline for Batch Zero in PGRR145 could already extend to 8 or 9 months (possibly


Vistra Comments || Project No. 58481                                                     Page 5 of 19
                                                                                                        5
 longer) once the commitment period, refinement study, and delays to the System Protection (Short-
Circuit) Analysis are taken into account, the Commission should reflect the 120-day window for
39.169 NMAs by amending proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(e) with new paragraph (5) as follows (in
addition to other proposed changes to this subsection discussed below):

        (e)         Interconnection study. Not later than 60 days after an intermediate
                    agreement is executed under subsection (d) of this section, the
                    interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must coordinate with
                    ERCOT to initiate an interconnection study.

              […]

                    (5)   An interconnection study conducted by ERCOT for a large load
                          subject to PURA § 39.169 and Section 205 of this Chapter must
                          be completed not later than the 120th day after ERCOT receives
                          all required information regarding the arrangement that is subject
                          to PURA § 39.169 and Section 205 of this Chapter.

        2. Exclusivity agreements for 39.169 NMAs satisfy site control for intermediate
              agreement.

        Another way that the Commission can help to recognize the unique characteristics and
procedural considerations of 39.169 NMAs, and to mitigate the impact of PURA § 39.169(d)
timeline disruptions from the combined effects of 16 TAC § 25.205, PGRR145, and this
rulemaking, the rule could recognize that 39.169 NMAs have a unique site control dynamic.
Specifically, 39.169 NMAs naturally require a significant amount of due diligence between the
existing generator and potential co-located large loads, given the physical and operational
coordination that such arrangements require and the long-term nature of such arrangements. Before
submitting an interconnection request, it is common for generators to review multiple potential
large loads and to enter into an exclusivity agreement with the large load that aligns most with the
generator’s needs and interests. The generator should conduct due diligence to ensure that the large
load has a viable path to site control, among many other quality screens and typically a monetary
exchange of value for entering that arrangement. Therefore, an exclusivity agreement with an
existing generator for a large load that will be a 39.169 NMA should provide an enhanced site
control demonstration (as well as provide a strong positive indicator for the large load’s power
supply, relevant to proposed paragraph (d)(7)).

        3. Financial security for 39.169 NMAs should only reach full scale following
            Commission approval of a 39.169 NMA application under PURA § 39.169 and
            16 TAC § 25.205.

        The proposed rule appropriately steps up financial security requirements as projects move
through the interconnection study process and become more likely to move forward. Vistra
supports that general approach. However, in the unique case of 39.169 NMAs, PURA § 39.169
and 16 TAC § 25.205 require additional studies and administrative review, including the risk of
denial or imposition of conditions that render a 39.169 NMA no longer viable despite material
dedication of capital and financial security by that point. As proposed, that financial security would
be non-refundable, even if the Commission were to deny a 39.169 NMA application.

        To better align the financial security escalation with the unique procedural considerations
of 39.169 NMAs, the Commission should not require the non-refundable financial security until
after an order approving the 39.169 NMA becomes final. The Commission should therefore amend
proposed 16 TAC § 25.205 paragraph (f)(7) by adding new subparagraph (C), as follows (or, in
the alternative, make the interconnection fee refundable based on the Commission’s order):

                        interconnection fee in the amount of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak
                        demand. An interconnection fee under this subsection is non-refundable.

        4. Power supply disclosure should also specify co-located generation and whether
            large load will receive retail electric delivery service from a DSP.

        Vistra supports the proposed rule’s provision that requires disclosure of power supply plans
as part of executing an intermediate agreement. A natural extension of that provision to include
disclosure of co-located generation and whether or not the large load would take retail electric
delivery service from a DSP would efficiently support integration of the unique characteristics and
procedural considerations for 39.169 NMAs that Vistra has highlighted in comments above.

        The Commission should amend proposed 16 TAC § 25.205 paragraph (d)(7) as follows:

B. The rule should be flexible to include the full diversity of large load configurations and
    only require DSP/TSP involvement as applicable (especially in intermediate and
    interconnection agreements).
        1. Definitions      of    Interconnecting    DSP,     Intermediate     Agreement,       and
            Interconnection Agreement should recognize that not every large load will take
            service from an Interconnecting DSP and allow any co-located generation entity
            to be a party to the agreement.

        There are several scenarios in which an interconnecting large load will not take retail
electric delivery service, and therefore requiring an Interconnecting DSP to be a party to an
Intermediate Agreement or Interconnection Agreement would not be appropriate. Such scenarios




Vistra Comments || Project No. 58481                                                     Page 8 of 19
                                                                                                        8
 may include self-service, 3 self-generators, 4 incidence of employment or tenancy, 5 electric
generation equipment lessor or operator arrangements, 6 non-settled generators, 7 “connected
island” and “export-only” approaches to self-limiting new co-located generation (“BYOG”)
facilities, 8 and possibly others. These are each typically very fact-specific cases, for instance,
applicability may vary depending on factors such as whether the large load is designed to consume
power from the grid (e.g., a large load co-located and netted with a solar facility that does not
curtail at night will take retail electric delivery service when the sun is not shining, but a large load
co-located and netted with an “export-only” dispatchable generator might not) as well as whether
the large load is located in an area that is singly-certificated to a municipally owned utility or an
electric cooperative with exclusive jurisdiction in that area.

        Generally, these scenarios are typically the exception: consider that 89% of the current
large load interconnection queue requests are not co-located, 9 and material posted for the April 20,

that total, many of which are co-locating with batteries, solar, and wind, 10 which in turn implies
that they will necessarily take retail electric delivery service. Therefore, the rule need not take on
significant changes to accommodate the minority of large load projects that would not take retail
electric delivery service – rather, simply acknowledging that such scenarios exist and including
rule flexibility to avoid risks of an unnecessary regulatory gap that could arise from requiring an

 C. The rule should fairly raise the bar for large load interconnections, particularly the
    largest ones.
        1. Large loads above a threshold size should have higher up-front financial security
            requirements, paired with greater refundability, to demonstrate access to capital
            needed to develop in tandem with or ahead of transmission buildout to support
            fair transmission cost allocation.

        Vistra supports robust financial commitment criteria that can help demonstrate that an
interconnecting large load has the access to capital and other means necessary to execute on an

                     VISTRA’S COMMENTS – EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Large loads subject to PURA § 39.169 and 16 TAC § 25.205 (“39.169 NMAs”) are a small subset
of the large load interconnection queue, but have both (1) specific statutory timing requirements
and (2) unique flexibility, transparency, and cost-effectiveness characteristics that warrant
prioritization in both Batch Zero (PGRR145) and this rulemaking.
    • 39.169 NMAs are effectively required to provide load flexibility in emergencies
    • 39.169 NMAs will provide real-time load telemetry to ERCOT, unlike other large loads
    • 39.169 NMAs generally require less transmission infrastructure in rate base to serve the load,
        but can contribute to cost recovery according to their use of the transmission system, reducing
        risk of transmission costs being allocated to other customers.

The rule should also account for unique procedural considerations of 39.169 NMAs.
   • Ensure interconnection studies for 39.169 NMAs comply with deadlines in PURA § 39.169(d).
   • Exclusivity agreements for 39.169 NMAs satisfy site control for intermediate agreement.
   • Financial security for 39.169 NMAs should only reach full scale following Commission
       approval of a 39.169 NMA application under PURA § 39.169/16 TAC § 25.205.
   • Power supply disclosure should also specify co-located generation and whether large load will
       receive retail electric delivery service from a DSP.

The rule should be flexible to include the full diversity of large load configurations and only
require DSP/TSP involvement as applicable (esp. in intermediate/interconnection agreements).
   • Definitions of Interconnecting DSP, Intermediate Agreement, and Interconnection Agreement
       should recognize that not every large load will take service from an Interconnecting DSP and
       allow any co-located generation entity to be a party to the agreement.
   • Definition of Interconnecting TSP should specify that for large loads co-located with
       generation resources, the Interconnecting TSP is the generator’s interconnecting TSP.

The rule should fairly raise the bar for large load interconnections, particularly the largest ones.
   • Large loads above a threshold size should have higher up-front financial security requirements,
       paired with greater refundability, to demonstrate access to capital needed to develop in tandem
       with or ahead of transmission buildout to support fair transmission cost allocation.
   • Financial security should be refunded over a longer time window. A large load minimum
       demand charge could also help ensure large loads pay their fair share of upgrade costs.

Miscellaneous Comments
   • Applicability to expanded interconnections should clarify 75 MW is the expansion interval.
   • Include references to both ERCOT’s Protocols and Planning Guide.
   • CLR designations should reflect registration and operation, not modeling.
   • Reallocation provisions should be worded to avoid potential for creating future “do-loops.”

Large loads subject to PURA § 39.169 and 16 TAC § 25.205 ("39.169 NMAs") are a small subset
of the large load interconnection queue, but have both (1) specific statutory timing requirements
and (2) unique ilexibility, transparency, and cost-effectiveness characteristics that warrant
prioritization in both Batch Zero (PGRR145) and this rulemaking.
     • 39.169 NMAs are effectively required to provide load flexibility in emergencies
     • 39.169 NMAs will provide real-time load telemetry to ERCOT, unlike other large loads
     • 39.169 NMAs generally require less transmission infrastructure in rate base to serve the load,
         but can contribute to cost recovery according to their use of the transmission system, reducing
         risk of transmission costs being allocated to other customers.

The rule should also account for unique procedural considerations of 39.169 NMAs.
   • Ensure interconnection studies for 39.169 NMAs comply with deadlines in PURA § 39.169(d).
   • Exclusivity agreements for 39.169 NMAs satisfy site control for intermediate agreement.
   • Financial security for 39.169 NMAs should only reach full scale following Commission
       approval of a 39.169 NMA application under PURA § 39.169/16 TAC § 25.205.
   • Power supply disclosure should also specify co-located generation and whether large load will
       receive retail electric delivery service from a DSP.

The rule should be ilexible to include the full diversity of large load configurations and only
require DSP/TSP involvement as applicable (esp. in intermediate/interconnection agreements).
   • Definitions of Interconnecting DSP, Intermediate Agreement, and Interconnection Agreement
       should recognize that not every large load will take service from an Interconnecting DSP and
        allow any co-located generation entity to be a party to the agreement.
    •   Definition of Interconnecting TSP should specify that for large loads co-located with
        generation resources, the Interconnecting TSP is the generator's interconnecting TSP.

The rule should fairly raise the bar for large load interconnections, particularly the largest ones.
   • Large loads above a threshold size should have higher up-front financial security requirements,
        paired with greater refundability, to demonstrate access to capital needed to develop in tandem
        with or ahead of transmission buildout to support fair transmission cost allocation.
    •   Financial security should be refunded over a longer time window. A large load minimum
        demand charge could also help ensure large loads pay their fair share of upgrade costs.

Miscellaneous Comments
   • Applicability to expanded interconnections should clarify 75 MW is the expansion interval .
   • Include references to both ERCOT's Protocols and Planning Guide.
   • CLR designations should reflect registration and operation, not modeling.
   • Reallocation provisions should be worded to avoid potential for creating future "do-loops."
